title: SLO-first autoscaler sweeps: latency vs. cost across regions (Jul 2026)
content:
Purpose:
This is an experimental sweep log for SLO‑driven autoscaling policies run across three regional GPU pools (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1). Goal: find operationally simple policies that keep p95 <= 250ms for short LLM tails (prompt+decode timeframe) while minimizing steady-state and burst cost. This doc is intentionally a working artifact: raw numbers, short notes, and concrete action items.

Background / motivation:
- Our current reactive autoscaler uses queue_length and GPU_util thresholds with aggressive downscale (cooldown 2m). We observe repeated p99 spikes during sudden traffic ramps tied to cold allocation and instance launch latencies.
- Product SLO target for most hosted customers: p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 1100ms (for gen endpoint, 1–2 second tails acceptable only for very large batches).
- Hypothesis: A lightweight SLO-first autoscaler (triggering on tail latency estimate + soft min pool) will reduce p99 spikes with small cost overhead vs. existing heuristic rules.

Experiment design summary:
- Sweep window: 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-12. Synthetic traffic generator replaying a mix of gen/chat traces (from customer-synth-traffic-v2).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (endpoint), token throughput, GPU_util %, queue_length, scale_events, cold_start_count, cost_estimated ($/hr).
- Policies tested (each run 4h, repeated 3x per region):
  A) Baseline current (queue_length > 20 -> scale up 1 instance; GPU_util > 78% -> scale up; min=0; cooldown up=30s/down=120s)
  B) SLO-lifted (p95_estimate > 250ms -> scale up step=+2; min=1; cooldown up=15s/down=300s)
  C) SLO + prewarm (same as B but with prewarm pool 1 per zone and prewarm_warmup=45s)
  D) Conservative-min (same as A but min=2, max step=+1, down cooldown=600s)
  E) Aggressive-burst (short cooldowns, step +4, min=0)

Key regional notes (env):
- us-west1: launch times median 48s, 95th 110s (spot-backed pools sometimes delayed)
- us-east1: launch times median 35s, 95th 80s (better zonal capacity)
- eu-west1: launch times median 72s, 95th 160s (intermittent TD-region throttling)

Results (aggregated median across 3 runs each):

1) Latency impact (p95/p99 in ms)
Policy | us-west1 p95 / p99 | us-east1 p95 / p99 | eu-west1 p95 / p99
-------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------
A (baseline) | 310 / 1400 | 280 / 1200 | 360 / 1800
B (SLO-lifted) | 240 / 950 | 220 / 860 | 260 / 1100
C (SLO+prewarm) | 220 / 480 | 210 / 420 | 230 / 520
D (conservative-min) | 260 / 900 | 245 / 820 | 275 / 1050
E (aggressive) | 280 / 1300 | 260 / 1100 | 310 / 1500

Notes: C shows the largest improvement on p99 because prewarm reduces cold starts. B and D both meet p95 <=250 in us-east1/us-west1; eu-west1 remains challenged without prewarm due to long launch times.

2) Cost delta (estimated $/hr relative to baseline A):
Policy | us-west1 | us-east1 | eu-west1
A (baseline) | 0% | 0% | 0%
B (SLO-lifted) | +9% | +7% | +12%
C (SLO+prewarm) | +14% | +12% | +19%
D (conservative-min) | +11% | +10% | +13%
E (aggressive) | +22% | +18% | +28%

Interpretation: SLO-first policies (B) increase steady cost modestly but sharply reduce p99 spikes in regions with reasonable launch times. Prewarming (C) further reduces tail latencies but adds 10–20% cost overhead. Aggressive policies (E) reduce some tail events at high cost and still suffer if launch times are long.

3) Cold starts and scale events:
- Baseline A: cold_start_count correlated with sudden 4x load ramps; us-west1 saw ~18 cold starts/hr during bursts.
- B: cold_starts reduced by ~45% vs A (fewer reactive jumps thanks to SLO estimator step-ups).
- C: cold_starts ~5/hr (prewarm masks most launches; warmup latency still visible when prewarm pool exhausted).
- D: few scale events but longer sustained over-provision. Downscale cooldowns prevented oscillation.

4) Oscillation and safety margin:
- Short down cooldowns (<=120s) produced flapping in queues when traffic has periodic spikes (customer-burst pattern).
- Increasing down cooldown to 300–600s dramatically reduced oscillation at cost of higher baseline.
- Step size capping (max +2) reduced overshoot events where many instances launched unnecessarily.

Operational learnings and constraints:
- Region-dependent behavior matters: eu-west1's long launch times make reactive-only strategies fragile. There we need either stronger min pools or prewarm guarantees.
- SLO-triggered scale-ups that are conservative in step size but faster in detection (p95 estimator) work best overall; combine with longer down cooldowns to avoid oscillation.
- Prewarm is effective for p99 but needs budget guardrails and better backfill logic when prewarm pool exhausted.
- Warmup timer of ~45s is the sweet spot for the model families we tested (Llama-2-13b variants quantized).
- Spot-backed instances increase launch variability; for SLO-first policies we should prefer zonal reserved capacity for critical pools or hybrid strategy with reserved prewarm.

Concrete recommendations (short‑term):
1) Roll out policy B (SLO-lifted) as default for hosted-api gen endpoints in us-west1/us-east1 with config: min=1, step=+2, cooldown up=15s, cooldown down=300s, max_step=2. (Owner: Maya Chen, INFRA-3421)
2) Enable prewarm (policy C) for high-SLA customers / enterprise plans in eu-west1 and other slow-launch regions. Prewarm sized: 1 per zone per pool. Add budget cap per pool. (Owner: Liam O'Connor, INFRA-3499)
3) Increase telemetry on cold_start attribution (which pool/zone/spot-reserved -> correlate with allocation events). Instrumentation ticket: add cold_start_reason tag to traces. (Owner: Noah Brooks)
4) Implement step-size caps and adaptive cooldown tuning: use moving-average of request rate to temporarily relax down cooldown after sustained low traffic. (Owner: Sofia Martinez)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does prewarm interact with Dedicated/GPU-reserved customers? (cost sharing and allocation semantics).
- Explore hybrid reserved + spot prewarm: reserved instances as thin prewarm layer to avoid spot variability.
- Need A/B tests on real production traffic (select small percent of customers) — synthetic replay may under/overestimate tail behavior.
- Can we build a cheap, local p99 predictor (ML model) to decide when to scale pro-actively rather than reactive thresholding?

Action items (owners + target dates):
- INFRA-3421: Deploy policy B to canary (10% of gen endpoints) in us-west1/us-east1 by 2026-07-22 (Maya)
- INFRA-3499: Prewarm config and budget caps prototype in eu-west1 by 2026-07-28 (Liam)
- Telemetry: cold_start_reason tag + dashboard by 2026-07-21 (Noah)
- PR: infra autoscaler max_step and cooldown tunables API change (GH PR #512) by 2026-07-18 (Sofia)

Appendix: quick raw numbers excerpt (example run, us-west1, 2026-07-08 02:00–06:00):
- baseline A: p50=120ms, p95=310ms, p99=1400ms, cold_start=21, scale_events=34, est_cost=$8.6/hr
- B (SLO): p50=115ms, p95=240ms, p99=950ms, cold_start=11, scale_events=26, est_cost=$9.3/hr
- C (SLO+prewarm): p50=110ms, p95=220ms, p99=480ms, cold_start=4, scale_events=9, est_cost=$9.8/hr

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working note; numbers are not final accounting. Please comment if you want more granular per-model family breakdowns (we tested two: llama2-13b-q4 and redwood-open-7b).
- If you have customer traffic traces we should add them to the replay set (contact product-hosted-api).

-- End of sweep log --
